Circle Centers On Radical Axes

GeometryCirclesConstructions
Game: Three circles and three straight lines you can change by moving the circles.
How to play: Drag a middle dot to move a circle, or a dot on its edge to make it bigger or smaller. With the keyboard, focus a dot and use the arrow keys.
Look for the math

Move the circles and watch the three straight lines. Something surprising happens: once two of the centres sit on the lines made from the other two circles, the third centre is forced onto its line too. There is nothing to win here — the picture is a droodle you can take apart.

A line of equal power

For a point X and a circle with centre C and radius r, the power of X is |XC|² − r². The radical axis of two circles is all the points with the same power in both. It is perpendicular to the line joining their centres; when the circles cross, it is simply the line through the two crossing points. In the picture the three axes are drawn in different styles: solid for P and Q, dashed for Q and R, dotted for R and P.

Two clues force the third

Write a, b, c for the squared distances PQ, PR and QR. Saying P lies on the axis of Q and R means a − rQ² = b − rR². Saying Q lies on the axis of P and R means a − rP² = c − rR². Subtract the two equations and the radii of R cancel: b − rP² = c − rQ². That is exactly the statement that R lies on the axis of P and Q. The page's claim is true, and the logic test confirms it on hundreds of arrangements built to meet the first two conditions.

The meeting point

The three axes meet at one point O, the radical center. Each axis is perpendicular to the side of the triangle opposite its centre, so the axes are the triangle's altitudes. Their meeting point is therefore also the orthocenter of triangle PQR. The original applet works in whole pixels: a centre counts as "on" a line when it is less than one pixel away, which is why a dot can blink out if a circle is nudged by a tiny amount.

Try lighting up P and Q, then guess whether R will light up before you move the last dot. Press Hint to see the triangle whose altitudes are the three lines.
